The two biggest mistakes are watering into the crown and placing it in a dry, heated room. This guide fixes both, showing you how to water safely and build the humid pocket this rainforest fern demands.

Light

In the wild, Asplenium nidus grows as an epiphyte on tree branches in dappled jungle light. Indoors, it needs bright, indirect light. A north or east-facing window is ideal. Direct sun will scorch the broad, thin fronds, causing large bleached areas that turn brown and papery. In the short, dark days of a Northern winter, the fern's growth will slow, but it rarely etiolates. However, if the light is too low, the new fronds will be elongated and pale. Rotate the pot a quarter turn every week to ensure symmetrical growth. A bright bathroom window is the perfect spot because the light is often diffused and the humidity is naturally higher. If you must place it in a darker room, supplement with a full-spectrum bulb for 10 hours a day. For more on using artificial light effectively, see our guide on fixing leggy growth.

Temperature

This fern likes steady warmth: 18°C to 24°C (65°F–75°F). It can survive down to 10°C (50°F) but will suffer chilling injury if exposed to cold drafts. A window that leaks cold air in winter will cause the fronds to turn yellow and soft, particularly near the pane. Radiators positioned beneath windows blast hot, dry air directly onto the foliage, which rapidly desiccates the fronds. Keep the plant away from both extremes. A consistent temperature, without sudden fluctuations, is key to avoiding stress. Air conditioning in summer also creates a cold, dry draft that the fern dislikes.

Humidity

High humidity is the single most critical factor. Aim for 60%–80%. A centrally heated home in winter often falls to 30% relative humidity, which is a death sentence for this fern. The fronds lose moisture through transpiration faster than the roots can absorb it, leading to brown, crispy edges that spread inward. The best solution is to keep the plant in a bathroom or kitchen with good natural light and regular steam. Alternatively, invest in a room humidifier and place it near the fern. Pebble trays and misting provide marginal improvements but are rarely enough on their own. Grouping several plants together creates a humid microclimate as they collectively transpire water vapor. If your fern is already showing brown edges, our brown crispy tips guide can help you diagnose and reverse the damage.

Watering

The most important rule: water the soil, never the rosette. In the wild, rain falls from above and drains through the leaf bases, but indoors, stagnant water in the crown promotes bacterial and fungal rot that quickly kills the emerging fronds. Instead, pour tepid filtered water directly onto the soil at the base until it runs out the drainage holes, then discard the excess. Allow the top 1 cm of soil to dry slightly before watering again. The soil should remain evenly moist, like a wrung-out sponge, never sodden. In winter, reduce watering frequency slightly as the plant’s metabolism slows. Fluoride and chlorine in tap water can cause tip burn; use filtered or rainwater if possible. Underwatered ferns wilt and the fronds turn dry and crispy; overwatered ferns develop soft, dark lesions at the base and a foul smell from the soil.

Soil

As an epiphyte, Bird's Nest Fern needs a very loose, well-aerated mix that still holds moisture. A blend of equal parts peat moss (or coco coir), perlite, and fine orchid bark works perfectly. Peat provides acidity (pH 5.0–5.5) and water retention; perlite and bark create air channels. Dense, standard potting soil will suffocate the roots and lead to crown and root rot. When repotting, keep the soil level exactly at the base of the rosette; burying the crown will rot it.

Fertilizer

Ferns are very sensitive to fertilizer salts. Use a balanced, urea-free liquid houseplant fertilizer diluted to quarter strength every 4–6 weeks during spring and summer. Over-fertilising causes immediate brown, burned frond tips. Stop feeding completely in autumn and winter. Every 2 months, flush the soil with plain water to leach out any accumulated salts. Organic options like a very weak seaweed solution are gentle but must be applied even more sparingly. If you see a white crust on the soil surface, it's salt buildup; scrape it off and flush the pot.

Propagation

Propagation is challenging for home growers. Bird's Nest Ferns produce spores on the underside of mature fronds, but raising them to new plants requires sterile, humid conditions and patience. Division is possible only when the plant produces a separate pup at the base, which is rare. For most owners, buying a new plant is the most reliable option. If you do find a pup, carefully cut it away with a clean knife, keeping some roots attached, and pot it in a small container with the standard mix. Keep it in a humidity dome until established.

Repotting

Repot every 1–2 years in spring when the roots have filled the pot and growth has slowed. Bird's Nest Fern has a shallow, fibrous root system, so a wide, shallow pot works better than a deep one. Gently tease out the outer roots and replant at the same depth. After repotting, water lightly and keep the plant in a shaded, humid spot for a week. Never pack the soil tightly; the roots need oxygen.

Toxicity

Asplenium nidus is completely non-toxic to cats, dogs, and humans. It's one of the safest houseplants, so you can place it on low tables without worrying about pets chewing the fronds.

Common Problems

Brown, crispy frond edges: Low humidity or fluoride toxicity. Increase humidity and water with filtered water. Trim off dead tissue. Fronds turning yellow and soft: Overwatering, cold drafts, or water in the crown. Check the base and reduce watering. Black, mushy centre: Crown rot from watering into the rosette. Stop watering the crown, improve air circulation, and remove any rotted tissue. Small, deformed new fronds: Nutrient deficiency or inconsistent watering. Apply a very dilute, balanced fertilizer and keep soil evenly moist. Scale insects: Brown bumps on fronds. Scrape off and treat with neem oil.

Peat provides acidity (pH 5.0–5.5) and water retention; perlite and bark create air channels. Dense, standard potting soil will suffocate the roots and lead to crown and root rot. When repotting, keep the soil level exactly at the base of the rosette; burying the crown will rot it. Fertilizer Ferns are very sensitive to fertilizer salts. Use a balanced, urea-free liquid houseplant fertilizer diluted to quarter strength every 4–6 weeks during spring and summer. Over-fertilising causes immediate brown, burned frond tips. Stop feeding completely in autumn and winter. Every 2 months, flush the soil with plain water to leach out any accumulated salts. Organic options like a very weak seaweed solution are gentle but must be applied even more sparingly. If you see a white crust on the soil surface, it's salt buildup; scrape it off and flush the pot. Propagation Propagation is challenging for home growers. Bird's Nest Ferns produce spores on the underside of mature fronds, but raising them to new plants requires sterile, humid conditions and patience. Division is possible only when the plant produces a separate pup at the base, which is rare. For most owners, buying a new plant is the most reliable option. If you do find a pup, carefully cut it away with a clean knife, keeping some roots attached, and pot it in a small container with the standard mix. Keep it in a humidity dome until established. Repotting Repot every 1–2 years in spring when the roots have filled the pot and growth has slowed. Bird's Nest Fern has a shallow, fibrous root system, so a wide, shallow pot works better than a deep one. Gently tease out the outer roots and replant at the same depth. After repotting, water lightly and keep the plant in a shaded, humid spot for a week. Never pack the soil tightly; the roots need oxygen. Toxicity Asplenium nidus is completely non-toxic to cats, dogs, and humans. It's one of the safest houseplants, so you can place it on low tables without worrying about pets chewing the fronds. Common Problems Brown, crispy frond edges: Low humidity or fluoride toxicity. Increase humidity and water with filtered water. Trim off dead tissue. Fronds turning yellow and soft: Overwatering, cold drafts, or water in the crown. Check the base and reduce watering. Black, mushy centre: Crown rot from watering into the rosette. Stop watering the crown, improve air circulation, and remove any rotted tissue. Small, deformed new fronds: Nutrient deficiency or inconsistent watering. Apply a very dilute, balanced fertilizer and keep soil evenly moist. Scale insects: Brown bumps on fronds. Scrape off and treat with neem oil.","citation":{"source":"PlantSolve","canonicalUrl":"https://www.plantsolve.com/plants/birds-nest-fern-care/","lastReviewed":"2026-05-31","license":"CC BY-NC 4.0"}}

But within weeks, it has started shedding leaflets like green snow, leaving a bare, messy skeleton. The primary struggle for indoor growers is managing the fern’s high demand for humidity and soil moisture. Modern homes, particularly in winter when central heating is active, have dry air that desiccates the foliage and triggers rapid leaflet drop. This comprehensive guide will show you how to recreate the humid understory environment that Boston Ferns thrive in, resolving common care issues and keeping the foliage lush and green.

Light

In their native tropical habitats, Boston Ferns grow under the canopy of trees, receiving bright, filtered sunlight. Indoors, they need bright indirect light to maintain their lush, dense growth. An east or north-facing window is ideal, as it provides gentle morning sun without the harsh afternoon heat. Direct, unfiltered sunlight from south or west-facing windows will quickly scorch the thin, delicate leaflets, turning them yellow and crispy. If you only have drafty, bright windows, place the fern several feet back or diffuse the light with a sheer curtain. While they can tolerate moderate shade, placing them in dark corners will cause growth to become thin, leggy, and pale, and will accelerate leaf shedding. For advice on assessing light levels, see our guide on fixing leggy plants.

Temperature

Boston Ferns thrive in moderate indoor temperatures between 16°C and 24°C (60°F to 75°F). They are sensitive to extreme heat and cold. Temperatures below 10°C (50°F) can cause chilling injury, leading to dark, soft, or dropping fronds. Avoid placing the fern near cold window drafts in winter or direct paths of air conditioners in summer. Similarly, place it away from radiators, fireplaces, or heating vents, which blast hot air and quickly dehydrate the fronds. Steady, uniform temperatures are essential to prevent stress-induced leaf drop.

Humidity

High humidity is critical for Boston Fern health. They prefer relative humidity levels between 50% and 80%. When humidity drops below 40%, particularly during winter when indoor heating dries out the air, the fern transpires moisture faster than its roots can absorb it. The leaflets dry out, turn brown at the tips, and shed. To maintain humidity, run a humidifier nearby or group the fern with other tropical plants. Placing the pot on a tray filled with pebbles and water also helps, as the evaporating water raises local moisture. Moving the plant to naturally humid rooms like bathrooms or kitchens with good light is an excellent strategy. For more tips, check out our comparison on humidity trays vs humidifiers.

Watering

Consistent moisture is key to Boston Fern care. The soil should remain evenly moist, resembling a wrung-out sponge. Water the fern whenever the top 1 cm of soil feels dry to the touch. Pour water evenly over the soil surface until it drains out the bottom holes, then empty the saucer. Never let the soil dry out completely, as even a single day of bone-dry soil can cause massive leaf shedding. Conversely, avoid overwatering or leaving the pot in standing water, which deprives the roots of oxygen and leads to root rot. During winter, when plant growth slows, you can allow the topsoil to dry slightly more between waterings, but the core root ball must remain damp. If you notice yellowing leaves, read our guide on yellow houseplant leaves to help diagnose the issue.

Soil

To support consistent moisture without waterlogging, Boston Ferns need a loose, organic, well-aerated soil mix. A mixture of two parts peat moss or coco coir, one part perlite, and one part organic compost works perfectly. Peat moss provides the necessary acidity (pH 5.0 to 6.0) and water retention, while perlite creates air spaces to prevent compaction and allow drainage. Avoid using dense, standard potting soil, which packs down, suffocates the roots, and promotes fungal rot. When potting, ensure the crown of the fern sits slightly above the soil line to prevent rotting of the base.

Fertilizer

Boston Ferns are moderate feeders during their active growth period. Feed them every 4 weeks in spring and summer with a balanced, liquid houseplant fertilizer diluted to half strength. Over-fertilizing leads to salt buildup in the soil, which burns the roots and shows up as brown, crispy margins on the fronds. Do not fertilize in autumn or winter when the plant is semi-dormant. Every few months, flush the soil thoroughly with plain water to wash away accumulated fertilizer salts.

Propagation

Propagating Boston Ferns is relatively simple using runners (stolons) or root division. As the plant grows, it sends out thin, leafless runners that grow over the sides of the pot. When these touch soil, they grow roots and form new plantlets. You can pin a runner into a small pot of moist soil next to the parent plant; once rooted, sever the connection. Alternatively, propagate by division during repotting in spring. Carefully cut the root ball into sections using a clean knife, ensuring each division has several healthy fronds and a good root mass, then pot them up separately.

Repotting

Repot your Boston Fern every 1 to 2 years in spring, or when you notice roots wrapping around the bottom of the container, water running straight through, or the plant drying out very quickly. Ferns have shallow, fibrous root systems, so wide, shallow pots work better than deep ones. Choose a new pot that is 1 to 2 inches larger in diameter. Gently loosen the outer roots, place the plant in the new container, and fill in with fresh, organic potting mix. Water thoroughly and keep it in a shady, humid spot for a week to recover.

Toxicity

The Boston Fern is completely non-toxic to cats, dogs, and humans. It is certified safe by the ASPCA, making it an excellent choice for pet owners who want lush foliage without worrying about their curious animals chewing the fronds. Placing the fern in a hanging basket keeps it out of reach while showing off its beautiful arching form.

Common Problems

The most frequent issue is leaf shedding and brown, crispy leaflet margins. This is almost always due to dry air or underwatering; increase humidity and water more regularly. Yellow fronds can indicate overwatering, poor drainage, or a lack of light; adjust your watering schedule and ensure the pot has drainage holes. If you see a white crust on the soil, it is a sign of salt buildup; flush the soil with water. Pests like spider mites and scale insects can attack if the air is too dry; treat with neem oil and wipe the fronds with a damp cloth.

Overview

If you're after a plant that practically explodes with color, Bougainvillea is hard to beat. You'll see it everywhere in tropical and subtropical spots—draped over fences, climbing up pergolas, or even shaped into bonsai. What most people think are flowers? Those are actually colorful leaves called bracts. The real flowers are the tiny white bits tucked inside. But hey, who's counting—they're gorgeous either way.

This vine comes from South America, so it loves heat, hates soggy roots, and demands full-on sun. Once it's settled in, it's surprisingly drought-tolerant and can push out those vibrant blooms multiple times a year if you treat it right.

Sunlight Requirements

Here's the honest truth: Bougainvillea is a sun junkie. It needs at least 6–8 hours of direct sun every single day to really show off. Skimp on that, and you'll get weak growth and hardly any of those colorful bracts. Put it in the brightest spot you've got—preferably outdoors—and make sure air can flow around it. That's the secret sauce.

Watering Guide

Most people kill Bougainvillea with kindness—too much water. You want to water deeply, then wait until the soil feels dry a couple inches down before you even think about watering again. Keep it on the drier side. Constantly wet soil? That's a fast track to root rot, yellow leaves, and a very unhappy plant.

Soil Requirements

Drainage is everything. If your soil holds water like a sponge, you're in trouble. Go for a gritty, fast-draining mix. Bougainvillea isn't too picky about pH, but slightly acidic to neutral works best. Just don't let those roots sit in a puddle.

Pruning and Flowering

Here's something cool: Bougainvillea blooms on new growth. So regular pruning isn't just about shaping—it actually triggers more flowers. After each round of blooms, give it a light trim. That'll encourage fresh shoots and another wave of color. Don't be shy, but don't butcher it either.

Obsessed yet? Same. We've got a whole sister site—bougainvillea.online—where we geek out on advanced pruning tricks, rare cultivar reviews, and tips for your specific climate. Go check it out if you want to go down the rabbit hole.

Overview

The Burro's Tail (Sedum morganianum), also known as the Donkey Tail plant, is a visually stunning trailing succulent native to southern Mexico. It is famous for its long, thick stems completely covered in fleshy, teardrop-shaped leaves that overlap like scales. When mature, these heavy, trailing stems can reach three to four feet in length, making it a spectacular specimen for hanging baskets.

However, it has one major quirk that frustrates many indoor gardeners: the leaves fall off if you look at them the wrong way. This is not necessarily a sign of poor health; it is an evolutionary adaptation. In the wild, animals brushing past the plant knock the leaves off, which then root in the ground below to create new plants. To succeed with a Burro's Tail indoors, you must place it where it will never be bumped or moved, give it blasting sun, and largely ignore it.

Light Requirements

This is a true sun-lover. A Burro's Tail requires the brightest light you can provide indoors. A south or west-facing window where it receives at least 4 to 6 hours of direct sunlight is mandatory. If you place it in a dim room or a north-facing window, the stems will stretch out (etiolate), leaving large gaps between the leaves, and it will become weak and pale green.

Watering Strategy

Like most thick-leaved succulents, the Burro's Tail stores massive amounts of water in its foliage to survive long droughts. Because of this, overwatering is the fastest way to kill it. You must allow the soil to dry out completely—100% bone dry—before watering again.

The best indicator that it needs water is the plant itself. When it is fully hydrated, the leaves are plump and rigid. When it is thirsty, the leaves will begin to look slightly wrinkled, puckered, or less firm. Once you see this sign, soak the soil thoroughly until water runs out the bottom of the pot, then wait for the cycle to repeat.

Temperature and Humidity

Typical household temperatures are fine, ideally between 65°F and 85°F (18°C - 29°C). During the winter, it can tolerate cooler temperatures down to 50°F (10°C), which can actually encourage it to bloom in the summer. It requires no extra humidity and perfectly tolerates the dry winter air of centrally heated Western homes.

Soil and Potting

Drainage is absolutely critical. Standard potting soil will hold too much moisture and rot the roots. You must use a dedicated cactus/succulent mix, ideally amended with 50% pumice, perlite, or coarse sand to ensure water drains instantly. Because the trailing stems become extremely heavy and brittle, you should repot this plant as infrequently as possible to avoid breaking it.

Fertilizing

This succulent is a slow grower and a very light feeder. Over-fertilizing can lead to weak, leggy growth. Feed it only once or twice a year during the spring and summer using a liquid cactus fertilizer diluted to half strength.

Propagation

While frustrating when they fall off accidentally, the fragile leaves make propagation incredibly easy. Simply collect the fallen leaves, let them sit on a dry surface for a few days so the broken end calluses over, and then lay them flat on top of slightly moist succulent soil. Keep them in a bright, warm spot out of direct sun. Within a few weeks, tiny pink roots will emerge, followed by a microscopic new plant.

Toxicity

Burro's Tail is entirely non-toxic to cats, dogs, and humans. However, due to its fragile nature, you will want to keep it well out of reach of curious pets who might bat at the trailing stems and knock all the leaves off.

Common Problems

Leaves Falling Off Constantly: If it happens when you touch it, it's normal. If the leaves are turning yellow, turning mushy, and falling off on their own without being touched, you are overwatering. Stop immediately and let the soil dry out.

Shriveled, Wrinkled Leaves: The plant is thirsty. Give it a deep, thorough soaking.

Stretching/Gaps Between Leaves: The plant is etiolated due to insufficient light. You cannot \"fix\" the stretched portions, but moving it to a brighter window will ensure the new growth comes in compact and healthy.

Overview

The Caladium, commonly known as Angel Wings or the Heart of Jesus, produces some of the most spectacularly colorful foliage in the entire plant kingdom. Native to the tropical rainforests of South America, it grows massive, paper-thin, arrow-shaped leaves that look like stained glass. The leaves are wildly painted in intense shades of neon pink, deep ruby red, brilliant white, and dark green.

While they are frequently grown outdoors in summer shade gardens, they make breathtaking indoor statement plants. However, growing a Caladium indoors requires understanding a critical aspect of their biology: they are not evergreen. They grow from an underground tuber (bulb). They put on a massive, explosive show of color all summer long, and then completely die back to the soil to sleep all winter. You must understand this dormancy cycle, or you will accidentally throw a perfectly healthy sleeping bulb into the trash.

The Winter Dormancy Panic

Every autumn, thousands of new Caladium owners panic. As the days grow shorter and temperatures drop slightly, the massive, beautiful leaves will begin to droop, turn yellow, and die one by one. The plant looks like it is failing.

Do not water it more. Do not fertilize it. The plant is simply going to sleep.

This is a natural, unavoidable dormancy. Once all the leaves have died, cut them off at the soil line. Stop watering completely. If you water the dormant bulb in the winter, it will rot and turn to mush. Store the dry pot in a warm, dark closet (above 65°F). In the spring, bring the pot back to a bright window, begin watering again, and within a few weeks, brand new spears will shoot up from the soil to start the cycle over.

Light Requirements: Fueling the Color

To produce their shocking neon colors, Caladiums require very bright, indirect light. An east-facing window is ideal. If you place the plant in a dark room, the leaves will emerge mostly green and leggy.

However, the leaves are literally paper-thin. They have absolutely zero protection against harsh heat. If you place a Caladium in a west or south-facing window with direct afternoon sun, the leaves will instantly scorch, bleach out, and develop massive, crispy brown burn holes.

Watering and Humidity (During Summer)

During their active summer growing phase, Caladiums are incredibly thirsty. The massive leaves transpire water rapidly. You must keep the soil evenly moist at all times. Water thoroughly the moment the top inch of the soil feels dry. If the soil dries out completely, the plant will collapse dramatically onto the floor.

They also require high humidity. If the indoor air drops below 50% humidity, the delicate edges of the leaves will crisp up. Keep the plant near a room humidifier or in a bright, humid bathroom.

Soil and Potting

Because they need to stay moist but rot easily, the soil must be rich but well-draining. A high-quality potting mix heavily amended with peat moss for moisture retention and perlite for drainage is perfect. Because they grow from bulbs, they prefer a wide, shallow pot rather than a deep one.

Toxicity

Caladiums belong to the Araceae family and are packed with insoluble calcium oxalate crystals. They are highly toxic to cats, dogs, and humans. If a pet bites into a leaf or stem, the microscopic crystals embed in the mouth and throat, causing immediate, excruciating pain, severe swelling, and vomiting. Keep them safely out of reach.

Overview

The Calathea Orbifolia (recently reclassified as Goeppertia orbifolia) is one of the most highly sought-after indoor plants due to its massive, round leaves adorned with striking metallic silver stripes. Native to the humid understory of the Bolivian rainforest, it is accustomed to filtered light, constant moisture, and thick, humid air.

While it is an absolutely stunning statement piece, it has earned a reputation for being somewhat difficult to keep pristine in standard Western homes. Central heating in the winter and air conditioning in the summer strip the air of the moisture this plant desperately needs, leading to its most famous complaint: crispy, brown leaf edges. However, by mastering its watering and humidity requirements, you can keep an Orbifolia looking lush and vibrant.

Light Requirements

In its native habitat, the Orbifolia grows on the forest floor, protected by the canopy above. Indoors, it needs bright, indirect light. An east-facing window that gets gentle morning sun or a north-facing window is ideal. You must protect it from harsh, direct afternoon sunlight, which will quickly bleach the beautiful silver striping and scorch the delicate leaves.

Watering: The Filtered Water Rule

Calatheas are notoriously dramatic when it comes to water quality. Municipal tap water in North America and Europe often contains chlorine, chloramine, fluoride, and heavy minerals. The Orbifolia cannot process these chemicals; it pushes them to the tips and edges of its leaves, resulting in chemical burns (brown, crispy edges).

You must use filtered, distilled, or rainwater.

The soil should be kept \"evenly moist.\" Do not let the pot dry out completely, but do not let it sit in a saucer of water, which will cause root rot. Water thoroughly when the top inch or two of soil feels dry to the touch.

Temperature and Drafts

Keep your Orbifolia in a warm room between 65°F and 80°F (18°C - 27°C). It is highly sensitive to sudden temperature changes. Keep it well away from drafty winter windows, exterior doors, and direct blasts from heating vents or AC units.

Humidity: The Non-Negotiable

This is a high-humidity plant. It requires ambient humidity levels above 60% to thrive and prevent leaf curling and browning. Typical indoor winter humidity often drops to 20-30%, which will cause the plant to struggle. Misting the leaves is ineffective and can promote fungal diseases. The best solution is to place a dedicated humidifier near the plant or keep it in a bright, humid bathroom.

Soil and Potting

The ideal soil mix must strike a delicate balance: it needs to retain moisture without becoming waterlogged. A mix of 50% high-quality potting soil, 30% perlite (for drainage), and 20% orchid bark or coco coir works perfectly. Repot only when the plant is completely root-bound, usually every 1 to 2 years in the spring.

Fertilizing

Because they are so sensitive to mineral salts, use a very light hand with synthetic fertilizers. Feed the plant once a month during the active growing season (spring and summer) using a balanced liquid fertilizer diluted to quarter-strength. Alternatively, top-dressing the soil with organic worm castings in the spring provides gentle, safe nutrients.

Toxicity

One of the best features of the entire Marantaceae family is that they are completely non-toxic to cats, dogs, and humans. It is a perfectly safe addition to a pet-friendly home.

Common Problems

Crispy Brown Edges: The number one issue. Caused by tap water chemicals, low humidity, or underwatering. Switch to distilled water and run a humidifier.

Leaves Curling Inward: The plant is severely dehydrated. It is attempting to reduce its surface area to stop moisture loss. Check the soil; if it is bone dry, soak it immediately. If the soil is wet, the roots may have rotted, preventing the plant from taking up water.

Faded Colors/No New Growth: This usually indicates that the plant is not receiving enough bright indirect light. Move it closer to a window, but out of direct sun.

Native to the dense, dripping understory of Colombian and Venezuelan rainforests, the Calathea ornata evolved in an environment of constant, high humidity, warm temperatures, and consistently moist soil fed by pure rainwater. When we place it in a climate-controlled home with dry central heating and water it from the tap, the plant goes into shock. Mastering Calathea care requires you to manage two critical factors: the moisture in the air and the chemicals in your water.

Light

As a forest floor dweller, the Calathea ornata requires medium to bright indirect light. An east-facing window where it receives gentle morning sun, or a spot several feet back from a bright south or west window, is ideal. Direct, harsh sunlight will rapidly bleach the leaves, fade the pink pinstripes, and scorch the edges. Conversely, if the light is too low, the plant will stop growing and the vivid colors will become muted.

Temperature

This tropical plant demands warmth and stability. It thrives in temperatures between 65°F and 80°F (18°C - 27°C). It is incredibly sensitive to cold drafts and sudden temperature fluctuations. A draft from a poorly sealed window in the winter, or a direct blast from an air conditioning vent in the summer, will cause the leaves to curl and drop. Ensure the temperature remains consistently above 60°F (15°C).

Humidity

Humidity is the single biggest challenge in keeping a Calathea looking pristine. They crave high humidity, ideally between 60% and 80%. When the air in a typical home drops to 30% or 40% (especially during the winter), the plant loses moisture through its large leaves faster than the roots can absorb it, resulting in the classic brown, crispy edges. To succeed with this plant, you must run a room humidifier nearby. Misting is ineffective as it only raises humidity temporarily and invites fungal infections.

Watering and Water Quality

Calatheas are highly sensitive to the chemicals (chlorine, chloramine, fluoride) and heavy minerals found in municipal tap water. Using tap water will almost certainly cause chemical burns on the leaf tips and margins. You must water your Calathea with distilled water, rainwater, or water purified by reverse osmosis. \n\nRegarding frequency, Calatheas prefer their soil to be evenly and consistently moist, like a damp sponge. Never let the soil dry out completely, but never let it become soggy. Check the soil every few days and water thoroughly when the top 1 inch feels dry. If the leaves curl inward into tight tubes, the plant is desperately thirsty.

Soil

A potting mix that retains moisture while still draining excess water is crucial. A standard indoor potting soil mixed with a generous amount of peat moss or coco coir for moisture retention, and 20-30% perlite to ensure the roots can breathe, creates the perfect environment.

Fertilizer

Calatheas are sensitive to the mineral salts in synthetic fertilizers, which can build up in the soil and burn the roots, causing brown leaf edges. Feed sparingly. Apply a liquid houseplant fertilizer, diluted to one-quarter strength, only once a month during the spring and summer. Do not fertilize during the fall and winter.

Propagation

You cannot propagate a Calathea from a stem or leaf cutting. They must be propagated by root division. The best time to do this is during repotting in the spring. Carefully remove the plant from its pot and gently tease the root ball apart, separating the plant into smaller clumps. Ensure that each new division has a healthy portion of the root system and several leafy stems attached.

Repotting

Calatheas do not like having their roots disturbed and generally only need repotting every 1 to 2 years, or when you notice roots growing out of the bottom drainage holes. When repotting, only go up one pot size (1 to 2 inches wider in diameter). A pot that is too large will hold too much wet soil, leading to root rot.

Toxicity

One of the greatest benefits of the Calathea ornata is that it is completely non-toxic to cats, dogs, and humans. It is entirely safe to keep in a home with curious pets, although the delicate leaves are easily damaged by playful swatting.

Common Problems

Brown, crispy leaf edges are practically guaranteed if humidity is too low or if you use tap water. Yellowing leaves, particularly at the base of the plant, indicate overwatering and root rot. Like many thin-leaved tropicals, Calatheas are susceptible to spider mites, which thrive in hot, dry air. Inspect the undersides of the leaves regularly for fine webbing or tiny, dust-like specks. If you spot them, wipe the leaves down immediately and treat with an insecticidal soap or neem oil.

Overview

The Rattlesnake Plant (Goeppertia insignis, formerly and still widely known as Calathea lancifolia) is one of the most eye-catching houseplants in existence. It features tall, upright, sword-shaped leaves with highly ruffled, wavy edges. The top of the leaf is pale green and patterned with alternating dark green ovals that look exactly like the skin of a rattlesnake. As a dramatic contrast, the entire underside of the leaf is a deep, glowing burgundy purple.

Because it belongs to the Marantaceae (Prayer Plant) family, it is 100% pet-safe. However, Calatheas are infamous in the houseplant world for being high-maintenance divas. If you neglect its need for high humidity, or if you dare to water it with tap water from the sink, the Rattlesnake Plant will punish you by immediately turning its beautiful leaves brown and crispy.

The Tap Water Ban

Watering a Rattlesnake Plant with municipal tap water is the fastest way to ruin it. Tap water contains fluoride, chlorine, and heavy mineral salts. The plant has no biological filter for these chemicals; it absorbs them, pushes them to the extreme tips and edges of the leaves, and suffers severe chemical burns. This is the primary cause of the dreaded \"crispy brown edges.\"

You must water this plant exclusively with distilled water, reverse-osmosis water, or rainwater. Additionally, because it is so sensitive to salts, if you use synthetic fertilizer, you must dilute it to 1/4 of the recommended strength to prevent fertilizer burn.

Watering: The Damp Sponge Rule

The Rattlesnake Plant cannot tolerate drought. You must keep the soil consistently, evenly moist at all times—exactly like a wrung-out damp sponge. When the top 1 inch of soil feels dry to the touch, it is time to water thoroughly.

If you let the pot dry out completely, the plant will violently curl its leaves inward into tight tubes to stop moisture from escaping, and the edges will crisp up immediately. Conversely, if you plant it in a pot with no drainage and let it sit in a swamp of mud, the roots will rot.

Humidity: Fighting the Crisp

Native to the Brazilian rainforest, this plant demands humidity levels between 60% and 80%. The air inside a typical centrally heated home drops to 30% in the winter. This dry air rapidly sucks the moisture right out of the thin, wavy leaves, causing them to turn brown and crispy.

Misting the plant is ineffective and can cause fungal infections. The only way to keep a Rattlesnake Plant looking pristine is to place a dedicated room humidifier directly next to it, or keep it in a bright, frequently used bathroom.

Light Requirements

In the wild, the Rattlesnake Plant lives on the jungle floor, completely shaded by the canopy. Indoors, it requires bright, indirect light to keep its intricate patterns sharp. An east-facing or north-facing window is ideal.

Never place this plant in direct sunlight. The delicate leaves will instantly scorch, the colors will bleach out, and the plant will curl up in distress.

The Prayer Movement

Like all Calatheas, the Rattlesnake Plant exhibits nyctinasty. In the morning, the leaves lay outward to catch the sun. In the evening, the plant dramatically folds its leaves straight upward like hands in prayer, showing off the vibrant purple undersides. This daily movement is controlled by a specialized joint at the base of the leaf called the pulvinus, and it is a wonderful indicator that your plant is healthy and thriving.

Overview

The Cast Iron Plant (Aspidistra elatior) earned its name during the Victorian era, a time when homes were dark, poorly ventilated, and filled with toxic fumes from coal fires and gas lamps. While most other plants perished in these harsh conditions, the Aspidistra thrived. Today, the most common frustration growers have with this plant is actually causing its demise through too much attention. This guide will teach you the art of \"benign neglect\" required to let this indestructible survivor flourish in your home.

Native to the dark forest understory of Japan and Taiwan, the Cast Iron Plant is built for endurance rather than speed. It utilizes an underground rhizome system to store energy and water, allowing it to survive long periods of drought and incredibly low light levels. When you bring this plant indoors, you are providing an environment that is likely brighter and safer than its natural habitat, which is why it is so forgiving of typical indoor stressors like dry winter air from central heating.

Light

This is the ultimate low-light houseplant. It is the perfect candidate for that dark corner of the bedroom or the windowless office cubicle that relies on fluorescent lighting. While it will survive in deep shade, it will grow slightly faster and produce larger leaves if placed in medium, indirect light. The only light requirement you must strictly adhere to is avoiding direct, harsh sunlight, which will quickly scorch the dark green leaves, turning them pale and scorched.

Temperature

The Cast Iron Plant is remarkably temperature resilient. While it prefers standard indoor temperatures between 60°F and 80°F (15°C - 27°C), it can tolerate drafts and temperature fluctuations that would kill a tropical Calathea or Ficus. It can survive drops down to 45°F (7°C) without significant tissue damage, making it an excellent choice for drafty entryways or unheated sunrooms during the winter.

Humidity

You do not need a humidifier for a Cast Iron Plant. Its thick, leathery leaves are excellent at retaining moisture, making it completely indifferent to the dry air generated by winter furnaces or summer air conditioners. It will perfectly adapt to whatever the ambient humidity is in your home, whether that is 20% or 60%.

Watering

Because it is usually placed in low light and grows very slowly, the Cast Iron Plant consumes water at a glacial pace. The biggest mistake you can make is watering it on a weekly schedule. You must allow the top 50% to 75% of the soil to dry out completely before watering again. During the winter months, you may only need to water it once a month. When in doubt, wait another week. It will easily survive being underwatered, but it will quickly succumb to root rot if kept continually wet.

Soil

While it is not overly fussy about soil, drainage is key to preventing root rot. A standard, high-quality indoor potting mix amended with a few handfuls of perlite to increase aeration is perfectly adequate. Avoid heavy, peat-dense soils that hold onto water like a sponge.

Fertilizer

Because the Cast Iron Plant grows so slowly, it requires very little nutritional supplementation. In fact, over-fertilizing is a common cause of brown, crispy leaf tips (fertilizer burn). Apply a balanced liquid houseplant fertilizer, diluted to half or even quarter strength, just once in the spring and once in the summer. Do not fertilize during the autumn or winter when the plant is dormant.

Propagation

Patience is required for propagation. You cannot grow a Cast Iron Plant from a leaf cutting; it must be propagated by division. This is best done in the spring during repotting. Carefully remove the plant from its pot and gently tease the root ball apart. Ensure that each new division contains a healthy section of the underground rhizome and at least two or three established leaves. Pot the divisions in fresh soil and water lightly.

Repotting

Do not rush to repot this plant. It actually prefers to be slightly root-bound, and because of its slow growth rate, it may only need repotting every three to five years. You will know it is time when the roots are severely circling the bottom of the pot or pushing the plant up and out of the container. When repotting, only increase the pot size by one to two inches in diameter. A pot that is too large will hold excess wet soil, leading to rot.

Toxicity

One of the greatest benefits of the Cast Iron Plant is its safety profile. It is completely non-toxic to cats, dogs, and humans. This makes it an ideal, worry-free floor plant for households with curious pets who like to chew on foliage.

Common Problems

The Cast Iron Plant is largely pest and disease-free. The most common issue is yellowing leaves, which is an unmistakable sign of overwatering and poor drainage. If you see yellowing, immediately reduce your watering frequency. If the leaves develop brown, crispy tips, it is usually a sign of either severe underwatering or a buildup of mineral salts from tap water or excess fertilizer. Flush the soil thoroughly with distilled water to remove the salts. Finally, because the leaves are large and broad, they tend to collect dust. Wipe them down with a damp cloth every few months to allow the plant to photosynthesize efficiently in low light.

Overview

The Fire Flash Plant (Chlorophytum orchidastrum, sometimes sold under the outdated name Chlorophytum amaniense) is an incredibly vibrant, show-stopping indoor plant native to the rainforests of East Africa. Also known as the Mandarin Plant, it is famous for its glowing, neon-orange petioles (the stems that connect the leaves to the base). The contrast between the bright orange stems and the wide, deep-green, slightly ruffled leaves is spectacular.

As a direct relative of the common Spider Plant, it shares an excellent safety profile, being completely 100% non-toxic to pets. However, it requires significantly more care than a standard spider plant. The glowing orange stems will rapidly fade to a dull green if the plant does not receive enough light, and its thin, wide leaves will turn brown and crispy if watered with hard tap water.

Light Requirements: Keeping the Orange

The brilliant orange color is not a permanent fixture; it is highly dependent on light. If you place a Fire Flash in a dim room or a dark office corner, the plant will survive, but all new stems will emerge completely green as the plant desperately tries to maximize chlorophyll production.

To maintain the neon-orange petioles, you must place the plant in very bright, indirect light. An east-facing window is ideal. However, you must avoid harsh, direct afternoon sun. The wide, thin leaves have zero protection against intense heat and will rapidly bleach out, scorch, and burn if exposed to direct rays.

Watering and Fluoride Toxicity

Watering requires a careful balance. The soil must be kept consistently, evenly moist, much like a damp sponge. Wait until the top inch of the soil feels dry to the touch before watering again. If you allow the pot to become completely bone-dry, the massive leaves will wilt drastically and the edges will crisp up permanently.

Important: Like its cousin the Spider Plant, the Fire Flash is exceptionally sensitive to fluoride and chlorine commonly found in municipal tap water. Using tap water will cause the tips of the leaves to burn and turn dark brown. To keep the foliage pristine, you must water this plant with distilled water, rainwater, or water filtered through a reverse-osmosis system.

Temperature and Humidity

Typical household temperatures between 65°F and 80°F (18°C - 27°C) are perfect. Keep it far away from freezing drafts and hot radiators. Because it has such large, wide leaves, it requires decent ambient humidity (around 50-60%) to prevent the edges from drying out. A nearby humidifier is highly recommended during the winter when central heating dries out the air.

Soil and Potting: Avoiding Crown Rot

The leaves of the Fire Flash emerge tightly from a central rosette at the soil line. Because this center area is so dense, it is highly susceptible to crown rot. You must use a well-draining potting mix (standard soil amended with 30% perlite) to ensure the base doesn't sit in mud.

Furthermore, when watering the plant, always aim your watering can at the soil around the plant. Never pour water directly into the center of the rosette, as water trapped in the dense crown will cause the entire plant to rot and collapse.

Flowering and Seed Production

During the summer, the plant will occasionally push out a short stalk bearing small, unremarkable white flowers. Unlike a Spider Plant, which uses these stalks to produce baby \"spiderettes,\" the Fire Flash will instead produce small seed pods. If you have no intention of germinating the seeds, it is best to snip the flower stalk off as soon as it appears. This redirects the plant's energy back into producing larger, more vibrant orange foliage.

Toxicity

The Fire Flash is completely non-toxic and pet-safe. Its bright colors and wide, floor-level leaves make it an excellent, worry-free statement plant for homes with curious cats or dogs.

To maintain the neon-orange petioles, you must place the plant in very bright, indirect light. An east-facing window is ideal. However, you must avoid harsh, direct afternoon sun. The wide, thin leaves have zero protection against intense heat and will rapidly bleach out, scorch, and burn if exposed to direct rays. Watering and Fluoride Toxicity Watering requires a careful balance. The soil must be kept consistently, evenly moist, much like a damp sponge. Wait until the top inch of the soil feels dry to the touch before watering again. If you allow the pot to become completely bone-dry, the massive leaves will wilt drastically and the edges will crisp up permanently. Important: Like its cousin the Spider Plant, the Fire Flash is exceptionally sensitive to fluoride and chlorine commonly found in municipal tap water. Using tap water will cause the tips of the leaves to burn and turn dark brown. To keep the foliage pristine, you must water this plant with distilled water, rainwater, or water filtered through a reverse-osmosis system. Temperature and Humidity Typical household temperatures between 65°F and 80°F (18°C - 27°C) are perfect. Keep it far away from freezing drafts and hot radiators. Because it has such large, wide leaves, it requires decent ambient humidity (around 50-60%) to prevent the edges from drying out. A nearby humidifier is highly recommended during the winter when central heating dries out the air. Soil and Potting: Avoiding Crown Rot The leaves of the Fire Flash emerge tightly from a central rosette at the soil line. Because this center area is so dense, it is highly susceptible to crown rot. You must use a well-draining potting mix (standard soil amended with 30% perlite) to ensure the base doesn't sit in mud. Furthermore, when watering the plant, always aim your watering can at the soil around the plant. Never pour water directly into the center of the rosette, as water trapped in the dense crown will cause the entire plant to rot and collapse. Flowering and Seed Production During the summer, the plant will occasionally push out a short stalk bearing small, unremarkable white flowers. Unlike a Spider Plant, which uses these stalks to produce baby \"spiderettes,\" the Fire Flash will instead produce small seed pods. If you have no intention of germinating the seeds, it is best to snip the flower stalk off as soon as it appears. This redirects the plant's energy back into producing larger, more vibrant orange foliage. Toxicity The Fire Flash is completely non-toxic and pet-safe. Its bright colors and wide, floor-level leaves make it an excellent, worry-free statement plant for homes with curious cats or dogs.","citation":{"source":"PlantSolve","canonicalUrl":"https://www.plantsolve.com/plants/chlorophytum-orchidastrum/","lastReviewed":"2026-06-01","license":"CC BY-NC 4.0"}}

Overview

The Corn Plant (Dracaena fragrans, sometimes sold as Mass Cane) is a ubiquitous, tree-like houseplant prized for its thick, woody canes and long, arching, striped leaves that resemble corn foliage. It is a staple in offices, malls, and living rooms because it is incredibly forgiving of neglect and low light. However, almost every grower eventually faces the same frustrating cosmetic issue: the tips of the beautiful leaves turn brown and crispy. This guide will teach you the specific watering requirements and the crucial water quality adjustments needed to keep this reliable giant looking flawless.

Native to tropical Africa, the Corn Plant is an understory shrub that is accustomed to filtered light and periods of dry weather. The thick, woody stems (canes) store moisture, making the plant highly resilient to drought but extremely vulnerable to being suffocated in heavy, constantly wet indoor potting soil. The key to Dracaena care is understanding that \"less is more\" when it comes to watering and fertilizing.

Light

Corn Plants are highly adaptable to various lighting conditions. They look best and grow steadily in medium to bright indirect light, such as an east-facing window or a few feet away from a south-facing window. They can survive for years in low-light environments, like a dark corner or a fluorescent-lit office, but their growth will be incredibly slow and the vibrant yellow/green stripes on the leaves may fade. Direct, hot afternoon sunlight must be avoided, as it will scorch the foliage and cause large brown burn marks.

Temperature

This tropical plant prefers standard household temperatures between 65°F and 80°F (18°C - 27°C). It is sensitive to cold drafts. Prolonged exposure to temperatures below 55°F (13°C) will cause the leaves to curl, turn gray, and drop. Keep it away from drafty winter windows and out of the direct path of air conditioning vents.

Humidity

Dracaenas are very tolerant of standard indoor humidity levels (40% to 50%). While they will appreciate slightly higher humidity, a room humidifier is rarely necessary unless your home is exceptionally dry (under 30%) during the winter. You do not need to mist the leaves.

Watering and Water Quality

Water quality is the single most important factor in Dracaena care. They are notoriously sensitive to fluoride, chlorine, and heavy minerals found in municipal tap water. Using tap water is the primary cause of those frustrating brown, crispy leaf tips. To prevent this, you must water your Corn Plant with distilled water, rainwater, or water purified by reverse osmosis.\n\nRegarding frequency, you must let the soil dry out significantly between waterings. Allow the top 50% of the potting mix to dry out completely. In a large 10-inch or 12-inch pot, this usually means watering only once every two to three weeks. When you do water, soak the soil thoroughly until water runs out the drainage holes, but never let the pot sit in a saucer of standing water.

Soil

A standard indoor potting mix is generally fine, but because it is crucial that the soil dries out between waterings, amending the mix with 20% to 30% perlite or pumice will vastly improve drainage. Heavy, water-retaining soils will cause the thick canes to rot.

Fertilizer

Corn Plants are very slow growers and require minimal feeding. Furthermore, they are highly sensitive to a buildup of fertilizer salts in the soil, which will burn the roots and cause brown leaf tips. Feed sparingly. Apply a balanced liquid houseplant fertilizer diluted to quarter strength only once or twice a year during the spring and summer. Do not fertilize during the fall and winter.

Propagation

Propagating a Dracaena is easy and is a great way to rejuvenate a plant that has grown too tall and \"leggy.\" You can propagate via stem cuttings. Simply cut the leafy top off the plant (leaving a few inches of bare stem attached). Let the cut end dry for a day, then place it in water or directly into moist potting mix to root. The original cane that you cut the top off of will sprout new growth points just below the cut, resulting in a branched, bushier plant.

Repotting

Because they grow so slowly and have a relatively small root system compared to their height, Corn Plants rarely need repotting. You generally only need to repot every three to five years, or when the roots are severely circling the bottom of the pot. When repotting, use a heavy pot (like terracotta or ceramic) that is only one or two inches wider in diameter; the weight will prevent the top-heavy plant from tipping over.

Toxicity

The Corn Plant is toxic to cats and dogs. It contains toxic saponins. If a pet chews on the leaves, it will cause gastrointestinal upset, vomiting (sometimes with blood), excessive drooling, and depression. Keep the plant out of reach of pets that are known to actively chew on houseplants.

Common Problems

Brown, crispy leaf tips are almost always caused by fluoride in tap water or a buildup of fertilizer salts. Switch to distilled water. You can safely trim the brown tips off with sterilized scissors. Yellowing, dropping lower leaves are a normal part of the plant's aging process as it grows a bare trunk. However, if multiple leaves turn yellow rapidly, or if the woody cane feels soft and squishy at the base, the plant is suffering from stem rot due to chronic overwatering.

Overview

The String of Buttons (Crassula perforata) is a wildly unique, architectural succulent native to the rocky slopes of South Africa. It is famous for its bizarre growth habit: it produces thick, fleshy, triangular leaves that grow tightly stacked in pairs directly on top of each other. Because the stem runs directly through the center of the paired leaves, it looks exactly like a string of green buttons threaded onto a wire.

When exposed to direct sunlight, the edges of the leaves blush a beautiful, vibrant pink or red. It is 100% non-toxic to pets, making it a highly sought-after plant for sunny windowsills. However, like all desert succulents, it requires strict watering discipline and massive amounts of light. If you treat it like a low-light houseplant, it will ruin its perfectly stacked appearance within weeks.

The Stretching Problem (Etiolation)

The entire appeal of the String of Buttons is its tightly stacked, compact appearance. If the plant does not receive enough direct sunlight, it will undergo a process called etiolation. The plant will panic, assuming it is trapped in the shade, and will rapidly stretch its stem upward to find the sun.

This stretching leaves massive, ugly, bare gaps between the leaves. Once a succulent stretches, it will never shrink back down. To fix an etiolated plant, you must use sterile scissors to cut the stretched top off entirely. Move the base of the plant to a south-facing window with direct sun, and it will push out tight, compact new growth. (You can also plant the cut top into dry soil to grow a second plant!)

Light Requirements: Sun Stressing

To keep the leaves tightly stacked, the String of Buttons must be placed in the brightest window you have. A south or west-facing window is mandatory. It thrives when receiving several hours of blazing, direct sunlight every day.

Furthermore, direct sunlight is required to maintain the beautiful red or pink borders on the leaves. This coloration is an active defense mechanism called \"sun stressing\" (the plant produces anthocyanins to act as a natural sunscreen). If the plant is kept in a dim room, it will completely lose the red borders and turn solid pale green.

Watering: The Squish Test

The stacked, fleshy leaves are essentially massive water storage tanks designed to survive months of drought in the African desert. Overwatering is the fastest way to kill this plant.

You must allow the potting soil to dry out 100% completely—all the way to the bottom of the pot—before watering. Never water on a schedule. Instead, gently squeeze the lowest, oldest leaves. If they feel rock-hard, the plant has plenty of water. If they feel slightly soft, pliable, or look wrinkled, it is time to water. When you do, soak the pot thoroughly until water flows out the drainage holes, then leave it completely alone until the soil is bone dry again.

Soil and Potting

Standard indoor potting soil will hold water like a sponge, suffocating the roots and causing the plant to turn yellow, mushy, and rot. You must use an extremely fast-draining cactus and succulent mix. Combine cactus soil with at least 50% perlite, pumice, or coarse sand to ensure that excess water drains away instantly. Always plant it in a pot with a drainage hole.

Toxicity

The String of Buttons is completely non-toxic and pet-safe. It is an excellent, worry-free addition to homes with curious cats or dogs, though its crunchy texture might invite unwanted nibbles.

Maintaining the same watering frequency as summer during this period is the most reliable way to kill it."}],"contentText":"Overview The String of Buttons ( Crassula perforata ) is a wildly unique, architectural succulent native to the rocky slopes of South Africa. It is famous for its bizarre growth habit: it produces thick, fleshy, triangular leaves that grow tightly stacked in pairs directly on top of each other. Because the stem runs directly through the center of the paired leaves, it looks exactly like a string of green buttons threaded onto a wire. When exposed to direct sunlight, the edges of the leaves blush a beautiful, vibrant pink or red. It is 100% non-toxic to pets, making it a highly sought-after plant for sunny windowsills. However, like all desert succulents, it requires strict watering discipline and massive amounts of light. If you treat it like a low-light houseplant, it will ruin its perfectly stacked appearance within weeks. The Stretching Problem (Etiolation) The entire appeal of the String of Buttons is its tightly stacked, compact appearance. If the plant does not receive enough direct sunlight, it will undergo a process called etiolation . The plant will panic, assuming it is trapped in the shade, and will rapidly stretch its stem upward to find the sun. This stretching leaves massive, ugly, bare gaps between the leaves. Once a succulent stretches, it will never shrink back down. To fix an etiolated plant, you must use sterile scissors to cut the stretched top off entirely. Move the base of the plant to a south-facing window with direct sun, and it will push out tight, compact new growth. (You can also plant the cut top into dry soil to grow a second plant!) Light Requirements: Sun Stressing To keep the leaves tightly stacked, the String of Buttons must be placed in the brightest window you have. A south or west-facing window is mandatory. It thrives when receiving several hours of blazing, direct sunlight every day. Furthermore, direct sunlight is required to maintain the beautiful red or pink borders on the leaves. This coloration is an active defense mechanism called \"sun stressing\" (the plant produces anthocyanins to act as a natural sunscreen). If the plant is kept in a dim room, it will completely lose the red borders and turn solid pale green. Watering: The Squish Test The stacked, fleshy leaves are essentially massive water storage tanks designed to survive months of drought in the African desert. Overwatering is the fastest way to kill this plant. You must allow the potting soil to dry out 100% completely—all the way to the bottom of the pot—before watering. Never water on a schedule. Instead, gently squeeze the lowest, oldest leaves. If they feel rock-hard, the plant has plenty of water. If they feel slightly soft, pliable, or look wrinkled, it is time to water. When you do, soak the pot thoroughly until water flows out the drainage holes, then leave it completely alone until the soil is bone dry again. Soil and Potting Standard indoor potting soil will hold water like a sponge, suffocating the roots and causing the plant to turn yellow, mushy, and rot. You must use an extremely fast-draining cactus and succulent mix. Combine cactus soil with at least 50% perlite, pumice, or coarse sand to ensure that excess water drains away instantly. Always plant it in a pot with a drainage hole. Toxicity The String of Buttons is completely non-toxic and pet-safe. It is an excellent, worry-free addition to homes with curious cats or dogs, though its crunchy texture might invite unwanted nibbles.","citation":{"source":"PlantSolve","canonicalUrl":"https://www.plantsolve.com/plants/crassula-perforata/","lastReviewed":"2026-06-01","license":"CC BY-NC 4.0"}}

Expect slower growth and some older leaves may yellow."}],"shortDesc":"After growing over 150 Croton specimens in UK and North American homes—where winter light is poor and radiators run full blast—over 10 years, we've mastered the exact light and stability tricks that keep leaves brilliantly colored and firmly attached.","content":"Your Croton entered your home a blaze of yellow, orange, and red, and now it’s a skeleton of bare twigs with a few green leaves clinging on. Crotons are famous for this dramatic leaf drop, and it nearly always comes down to a sudden environmental change—a cold draft, a dark corner, or even being moved from one room to another. This guide explains how to stabilise the plant’s world so it holds its color and its leaves.

Light

Brightness is the key to Croton color. The vivid yellow, orange, and red pigments are carotenoids and anthocyanins that develop in response to high light intensity. Without enough light, new leaves emerge green and stay that way, while the plant diverts energy into stretching its stems. Place your Croton in a south or west-facing window where it receives several hours of direct morning or late afternoon sun. A sheer curtain can diffuse the harshest midday rays in summer. In a dim Northern European winter, the plant will almost certainly lose some lower leaves as light levels fall—this is the plant shedding inefficient solar panels. A full-spectrum grow light positioned 30 cm above the foliage for 10 hours a day can keep color alive and prevent leaf drop. Do not move the Croton once you've found a spot it likes; they are notoriously sensitive to relocation and will drop leaves from the shock of a changed light angle or intensity.

Temperature

Crotons demand steady warmth: 20°C to 27°C (68°F–80°F) is ideal. They will protest at anything below 15°C (60°F) by dropping leaves. The most common killer is a cold windowsill draft. Even on double-glazed windows, temperatures can drop sharply at night. Place the pot 15–20 cm back from the glass in winter or use a thermal curtain as a barrier after dark. Equally damaging is the blast from a nearby radiator, which creates an ultra-dry hot zone that cooks the leaves and encourages spider mites. A consistent temperature, without sudden swings, is the only way to keep Croton leaves on the stems. Summer air conditioning also causes temperature shock; keep the plant out of the direct air stream.

Humidity

As a tropical lowland plant, Croton craves high humidity—60% to 80%. Indoor heating in winter can drop this to 30%. Low humidity causes leaf tips and edges to brown and crisp, and it also opens the door to spider mites, which are a Croton’s worst enemy. Use a humidifier in the room, set the pot on a large pebble tray, and group it with other plants to raise ambient moisture. Misting alone won’t suffice in a dry house, but it can help if done daily with tepid water, especially on the undersides of leaves where mites tend to congregate. A humid environment also reduces the shock from temperature fluctuations.

Watering

Water when the top 2 cm of the potting mix feels dry. Crotons like consistent moisture but hate wet feet. Use tepid, filtered water to avoid fluoride damage, which shows as brown leaf tips. Water thoroughly until it drains, then empty the saucer. During winter, reduce the frequency slightly to allow the top 3 cm to dry between waterings, matching the slower uptake. Underwatering causes leaf wilt and drop; overwatering causes root rot and the same leaf drop. The key is checking the soil with your finger each time. If the pot feels very light and leaves are drooping, water immediately. If the soil is damp and leaves are dropping, you’ve overwatered.

Soil

A well-draining, slightly acidic mix is essential. Combine 60% peat moss or coco coir, 20% perlite, and 20% coarse sand or fine orchid bark. This retains moisture without compacting, allowing air to reach the roots. Dense, heavy soil suffocates the roots and leads to rapid decline. When repotting, do not compress the soil; keep it light and fluffy.

Fertilizer

Feed every 4 weeks from March to August with a balanced liquid fertilizer (such as 10-10-10) diluted to half strength. Croton benefits from micronutrients like iron and magnesium to support color development, so choose a formula with trace elements. Stop feeding entirely in autumn and winter. Excess fertilizer salts in the soil will burn the leaf tips; flush the soil with plain water every 6-8 weeks to prevent buildup. Organic alternatives like compost tea work well but should be applied more frequently at quarter strength.

Propagation

Propagation is done by stem cuttings. In spring, cut a 10–15 cm length from a healthy tip with 3–4 leaves. Remove the bottom leaves, dip the cut end in rooting hormone, and insert into a pot of moist, equal parts perlite and peat. Cover with a clear plastic bag to maintain high humidity and keep in bright, indirect light. Roots should develop in 4–6 weeks. Croton sap is milky and can irritate skin, so wear gloves. Water propagation is less reliable for Crotons.

Repotting

Repot every 1–2 years in spring, just before the growing season. Signs include roots poking from drainage holes or the plant drying out too quickly. Choose a pot only 2–3 cm larger in diameter. After repotting, expect some leaf drop—this is normal. Keep the plant in the same location and maintain high humidity to minimize shock. For a detailed guide on reducing transplant stress, see our repotting shock rescue guide.

Toxicity

Codiaeum variegatum contains a toxic, milky sap that can cause skin irritation and is harmful if ingested. Keep it away from pets and children, and always wear gloves when pruning or handling broken stems. Wash your hands thoroughly after contact.

Common Problems

Mass leaf drop: Triggered by cold drafts, low light, or being moved. Stabilise conditions and wait; new leaves will appear. Green, lacklustre leaves: Insufficient light. Move gradually to a brighter spot. Brown crispy leaf edges: Low humidity or under-watering. Increase humidity and water more consistently. Fine webbing and stippled leaves: Spider mites. Mist regularly, apply neem oil, and raise humidity. Sticky residue on leaves: Scale insects or mealybugs. Dab with alcohol-soaked cotton. For the most common issue, read our guide on spider mite control.

Overview

The Crown of Thorns (Euphorbia milii) is a fascinating, semi-succulent shrub native to Madagascar. It features thick, water-storing stems completely covered in sharp, formidable spines. Despite its rugged, intimidating appearance, it produces delicate, teardrop-shaped green leaves and stunning, colorful blooms (which are technically modified leaves called bracts) in shades of red, pink, yellow, and white.

It is one of the few indoor plants capable of blooming year-round, making it highly prized for sunny windowsills. However, this is not a plant for everyone. It comes with two major warnings: first, its spines are sharp enough to draw blood, and second, it bleeds a highly toxic white latex sap when damaged. It must be handled with care and kept away from children and pets.

Light Requirements: Full Sun is Mandatory

If you want a Crown of Thorns to bloom, you must provide it with the brightest light possible. It requires a minimum of four to six hours of direct, unfiltered sunlight every day. A south-facing or west-facing window is non-negotiable. If you place it in a dim room or a north-facing window, the plant will survive, but it will grow weak, \"leggy\" stems, drop its lower leaves, and refuse to produce a single flower.

Watering Strategy

This is where many indoor gardeners fail. Because it looks like a cactus, people treat it like a cactus, withholding water for months at a time. While the Crown of Thorns is drought-tolerant, it will respond to extreme drought by dropping all of its leaves to survive. To keep it lush and blooming, water the plant thoroughly when the top 50% to 75% of the soil feels dry. During the heat of summer, this might be once a week. In winter, reduce watering significantly, allowing the soil to dry out almost completely.

Temperature and Humidity

Being native to Madagascar, this plant loves heat. Typical indoor temperatures between 65°F and 90°F (18°C - 32°C) are perfect. It is highly sensitive to cold; temperatures below 50°F (10°C) or exposure to a freezing window draft will cause it to drop its leaves immediately. It prefers dry air and has zero need for a humidifier, making it perfectly suited for centrally heated Western homes.

Soil and Potting

Excellent drainage is required to prevent root rot. Use a high-quality commercial cactus and succulent mix, or amend standard potting soil with 50% perlite or pumice. Always use a pot with a large drainage hole. Terracotta pots are excellent for Euphorbias because they breathe, allowing the soil to dry out faster.

Fertilizing

To support its continuous blooming cycle, the Crown of Thorns requires slightly more fertilizer than a typical succulent. Feed it once a month during the spring and summer using a liquid houseplant fertilizer diluted to half-strength. Look for a fertilizer slightly higher in phosphorus to encourage blooming. Do not fertilize during the winter.

Pruning and Toxicity Warning

Over time, the plant can become leggy and unruly. You can prune it back to encourage branching, but you must take extreme precautions. Like all Euphorbias, the Crown of Thorns contains a milky white latex sap that is highly toxic and severely irritating.

If this sap touches your skin, it can cause a painful rash or blistering. If it gets in your eyes, it can cause temporary blindness and severe pain. If ingested by cats, dogs, or humans, it causes intense vomiting and gastrointestinal distress. Always wear thick, leather gardening gloves and protective eyewear when pruning this plant. Wash your tools immediately afterward.

Common Problems

Leaves Dropping Suddenly: Usually caused by one of two things: letting the soil stay bone-dry for too long, or exposing the plant to a cold draft. Adjust your watering or move it away from the drafty window.

Yellowing Bottom Leaves: This is the classic sign of overwatering. Ensure the soil is drying out halfway down before watering again, and never let the pot sit in a saucer of standing water.

No Flowers: The plant is not receiving enough direct sunlight. Move it to a brighter window.

Overview

The Ctenanthe burle-marxii, often called the Fishbone Prayer Plant or the Never Never Plant, is a breathtaking, low-growing tropical native to Brazil. It features pale, silvery-green, oval leaves painted with striking, dark green alternating stripes that perfectly resemble a fish skeleton. When it folds its leaves up at night, it reveals a gorgeous deep burgundy-purple underside.

Because it is a member of the Marantaceae family (along with Calatheas, Marantas, and Stromanthes), it is completely pet-safe. However, it also shares the family's notorious reputation for being a high-maintenance diva. If you do not provide it with high humidity and pure, filtered water, it will quickly develop ugly, crispy brown edges that ruin its pristine appearance.

The Tap Water Ban

The absolute fastest way to ruin a Ctenanthe is by watering it from the sink. Municipal tap water contains heavy salts, chlorine, and fluoride. This plant has no biological mechanism to filter out these chemicals. As it drinks, it pushes the chemicals to the extreme edges of the leaves, where they build up and cause severe chemical burns. This manifests as brown, dry, crispy edges.

To prevent this, you must water the plant exclusively with distilled water, reverse-osmosis water, or rainwater. Furthermore, it is highly sensitive to synthetic fertilizer salts. If you fertilize, dilute it to 1/4 of the recommended strength to prevent fertilizer burn.

Watering: The Damp Sponge

Unlike succulents that want to dry out completely, the Ctenanthe needs its soil kept consistently, evenly moist—much like a wrung-out damp sponge. When the top half-inch of soil feels dry to the touch, water it thoroughly.

If you allow the pot to completely dry out, the plant will violently curl its leaves inward into tight tubes to prevent moisture loss, and the edges will crisp up immediately. Conversely, if you leave the pot sitting in a saucer of stagnant water, the rhizomes will rot. Consistency is the key to success.

Humidity and Temperature

Native to the humid rainforest understory, the Ctenanthe demands humidity levels between 60% and 80%. Standard indoor heating drops humidity to 30%, which will rapidly suck the moisture out of the thin leaves. You must run a dedicated room humidifier nearby. Misting the plant does not work and often leads to fungal leaf spot diseases.

Keep the plant in a warm room between 65°F and 80°F (18°C - 27°C). It is highly susceptible to cold drafts; a blast of cold air from an exterior door or an AC vent will cause the leaves to wilt dramatically.

Light Requirements

In the wild, the Ctenanthe lives on the forest floor, completely shaded by the canopy above. Indoors, it requires bright, indirect light to maintain the stark contrast of its fishbone pattern. An east or north-facing window is ideal.

Never place this plant in direct sunlight. The thin, delicate leaves will instantly scorch, and the pale silver-green sections will bleach out to a sickly, pale yellow.

The Prayer Movement

One of the most rewarding aspects of owning a Ctenanthe is watching it move. Thanks to a specialized joint at the base of each leaf called the pulvinus, the plant tracks the sun. In the morning, the leaves lay completely flat to absorb maximum light. As the sun sets, the plant folds its leaves straight upward, resembling hands in prayer. This circadian rhythm (nyctinasty) is a sign of a perfectly healthy, happy plant.
